hooks.text: A billion-light-year hole in space might be a cosmic bruise.
What could leave a billion-light-year scar on the edge of our universe?
There is a massive region of space where all matter simply vanished.

title: The Billion-Light-Year Void in Eridanus
description: Astronomers discovered an immense cosmic wasteland in the constellation Eridanus that might be a scar from another universe.

beats.text: A billion-light-year hole in space might be a cosmic bruise.
beats.visual: Artist concept of a multiverse bubble collision, 2015

beats.text: In 2004, astronomers scanning the Big Bang's ancient afterglow found a massive, unexpected anomaly.
beats.visual: NASA WMAP cosmic microwave background radiation map, 2003

beats.text: NASA's WMAP satellite detected a distinct Cold Spot in the constellation Eridanus that shouldn't exist.
beats.visual: Eridanus constellation star chart with Cold Spot overlay

beats.text: This supervoid spans nearly two billion light-years and is almost entirely empty of all normal matter.
beats.visual: Conceptual visualization of the cosmic web with a massive void
queries: large scale structure of the universe

beats.text: Ancient light photons lose energy as they cross this wasteland through the Integrated Sachs-Wolfe effect.
beats.visual: Integrated Sachs-Wolfe effect diagram showing photon energy loss, 2014

beats.text: The feature was so unexpected that some researchers nicknamed it the Axis of Evil.
beats.visual: ESA Planck satellite cosmic microwave background anomaly map, 2013

beats.text: One mind-bending theory suggests this massive gap is where our universe collided with a parallel one.
beats.visual: Scientific illustration of a collision between two bubble universes

beats.text: Such an ancient impact would leave a permanent scar.
beats.visual: Detailed map of the Cosmic Microwave Background showing the Cold Spot
